title: No one understands training intensity
summary: NH argues intensity is simply a number (percentage of max or RPE), not a feeling, aggression or bar speed, and is relative to each lifter. Bodybuilders should avoid 1RMs and instead gain intensity through reps, sets and accumulated fatigue (relative intensity) while staying in a 60-95% intensity window. Evolving rep ranges taken to failure capture intensity without calculating anything.
claims: Intensity is a number (percentage of 1RM or RPE), not a feeling; feeling intense or being aggressive in the gym has nothing to do with programming intensity
Screaming, collapsing after sets and theatrics by pros are often cardio fatigue or done for the camera; copying them does not make a set intense
Lifting speed does not indicate intensity or effort level; he lifts slowly, so a rep that looks like a max may leave five more in the tank
Intensity is relative to the lifter: 120 lb on the deadlift can be 30% for one person and 90% for a weaker one; you don't need big weights to train intensely
Lifters used intensity long before it was named; untutored lifters often train with more real intensity than those misled by online information
He prefers percentages over RPE but both are valid for bodybuilders
He hasn't tested a 1RM in about four years yet still programs by intensity
1RMs are bad for bodybuilding: maxing is a skill only powerlifters need and gives no hypertrophy benefit
A 1RM concentrates injury risk into one all-or-nothing rep at maximal load; an injury on rep 3 at 70% is far less severe
A double just below your max beats a single: e.g. 485 lb x2 instead of 500 lb x1 doubles tonnage with less injury risk and less fatigue
Tonnage is king for hypertrophy; strength is just a way to grow tonnage over time
Estimate your max from rep performance (e.g. 200 lb squat for 10) rather than testing it; bodybuilders should base intensity on reps
Absolute intensity is the load as a % of 1RM; relative intensity rises within a set as fatigue accumulates, so the last rep of an 80% set can feel like 100% while the joints only handle 80%
Intensity also rises across sets: the first rep of a second set at the same weight might be 81-82% instead of 80% because the muscle is pre-fatigued
Open sessions with the heaviest strength work; it pre-fatigues the muscle so later back-off sets (e.g. 3 hard squat sets then 3 back-off sets) are not junk volume
The intensity window for working sets runs from about 60% to 95-96% of max; sets at 20-60% are junk volume
Very light sets can't reach meaningful intensity: a 500 lb squatter cannot get the predicted 80-90 reps with 135 because lactic acid and pump stop him first
When accumulated fatigue pushes your sets out of the useful window, end the session and go home
Don't use relative intensity as an excuse for endless high-rep sets; fatigue can disguise junk volume
Three to four sets of fairly high intensity always beat one set of maximal intensity because repeatability means more tonnage, e.g. 3 sets at 240 lb beats 1 set at 250 lb on squats
A set's intensity is the sum of all its reps rising toward failure, so an RPE-7 start may average out to an 80% set
Hypertrophy training should be like a fartlek, repeated intense bursts with recovery, not one sprint; top sets are the sprints
An evolving rep range such as 4-8 taken to failure is itself an intensity bracket; his free programs never prescribe RPE or percentages
Frequency affects intensity: repeating the same squat set the next day is effectively more intense because you haven't recovered
Use reps in reserve as a safety tool to control intensity per lift: he goes to about 0 RIR on deadlifts but stays below 95% on squats
Bodybuilding intensity should be a steady fire sustained through the workout, not an explosion
exercises: taken to ~0 RIR with reps, never singles
keep below ~95%; leave reps in reserve; open the session with heavy sets then back-off sets
higher risk lift; pre-fatigue makes back-off sets productive
